context: Qaf is Makkan and argues one point, that the dead will be raised. Its audience had a settled objection, quoted in the third verse, that a man who has died and become dust is beyond any return. The surah answers with no miracle, pointing instead at what the objectors already accepted: a sky without a crack in it, mountains, layered palm trees, and rain falling on dead ground.

The Makkan setting shows in the compression. There is no legislation and no community to organise, the eight peoples of verses 12 to 14 are named without a story told of any of them, and what the surah spends its length on instead is the moment of death and what follows it.
name_story: The surah is named for the letter Qaf, which stands alone as its first verse and is followed at once by an oath by the glorious Qur'an. The title explains nothing, which is worth noticing: the disconnected letters are recited rather than decoded, and the earliest authorities did not agree on their meaning, several declining to say.

movements.note: The objection to a warner from among themselves, and to being raised out of dust, is answered with what is visible: a sky without flaws, mountains and gardens, rain reviving dead land. That last case is named as the pattern of the emergence from the graves.
Eight peoples are listed in three verses, from the people of Nuh to the people of Tubba', with nothing said of them except that they denied.
Allah's knowledge of what the soul whispers is stated, two recording angels are seated at right and left, and death arrives with the words that this is what he had been avoiding.

movements.h: The court and the two destinations
movements.note: A driver and a witness bring each soul, and Hell is asked whether it is full and answers by asking for more. Paradise is brought near, and the last word said of it is that with Him there is still more.

The heavens and the earth were made in six days with no fatigue touching Him, and the Prophet ﷺ is told to be patient, to glorify at both ends of the day, and to remind, since he was not sent to compel.

themes.t: Argument from what is already accepted
themes.d: Every proof offered for the resurrection is drawn from something the audience did not dispute. Rain on dead ground is the closest case, and the surah says of it plainly that the emergence is like that.

The two recording angels are seated immediately after the statement that Allah knows what the soul whispers, which makes the record a witness produced for the man rather than information supplied to his Lord.
Verse 22 describes the change at death as the lifting of something that had been in the way. Nothing new is disclosed; it is the eyesight that alters.

themes.t: Whoever has a heart, or listens
themes.d: The condition attached to benefit in verse 37 is attention rather than intelligence or standing, which fits a surah the Prophet ﷺ read weekly from the pulpit.

heart: Qaf can be read in one sitting, and it keeps the reader at close range throughout. The jugular vein, the whisper of the soul, an angel on either side, the intoxication of death: none of it is at a distance, and the lens never widens for long. The effect of attentive reading is a narrowing, since nearly everything described either is happening to the reader already or will.

The Prophet ﷺ read this surah from the pulpit every Friday, and one woman of Madinah said she learned it only from hearing him say it there. It was not kept for funerals or nights of fear but chosen for the ordinary weekly gathering of people who had come in from their work.

passages.why: Allah's nearness to man in a single clause, quoted constantly and rarely read in its setting, a sentence about knowing what the soul whispers.
Death described as an intoxication that arrives carrying the truth, addressed with the words that this is what you were avoiding.
The statement that the Day informs no one of anything new. What changes is the eyesight and not the facts.
The verse naming the condition under which a reminder works, describing two ways of being present and ruling out reading with neither.

connections.why: The Prophet ﷺ recited Qaf and Al-Qamar together at both Eids, and their content fits the pairing: Qaf argues that the Hour is coming, Al-Qamar recounts what became of those who waited for further proof.
Al-Qiyamah takes up the same objection about scattered bones and answers it with the fingertips, making the identical argument in a sharper register.

virtue.text: An authentic prophetic practice is attached to this surah, though not a stated reward for reading it. Umm Hisham bint Haritha said she learned Qaf only from the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who recited it every Friday on the pulpit, which is in Sahih Muslim 873. Muslim also records from Abu Waqid al-Laythi that he recited Qaf and Al-Qamar at the two Eids. These reports establish where the surah was read and how regularly, not a merit for the reciter.
virtue.src: Muslim 873; Eid recitation from Abu Waqid al-Laythi in Muslim
